Incubating eggs of the Yellow-tailed black cockatoo are maintained at a steady 36 °C [T = 36 °C] by the attending female, and under these thermal conditions, the embryo develops for a period ranging from 28 to 31 days [ab = 28 to 31 days] prior to hatching. Upon emergence, the freshly hatched nestling presents a modest wet weight at birth of approximately 26 grams [Wwb = approximately 26 grams], a value that reflects the substantial yolk reserves allocated to the altricial chick. This initial mass is the starting point for a prolonged period of parental care during which the nestling is entirely dependent on its parents for thermoregulation and food. The relatively short incubation period, combined with the small birth mass, is characteristic of many large-bodied parrots that produce small clutches but invest heavily in each offspring over an extended developmental phase. Field observations indicate that the temperature within the nest hollow during incubation can fluctuate slightly, but the parent bird maintains the clutch at the optimal developmental temperature with remarkable consistency, ensuring the 28-to-31-day incubation window is achieved across the majority of breeding attempts.

Under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic period of this species, typically around 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the developmental milestones of the nestling proceed on a predictable schedule. The dependent chick remains within the nest cavity until it achieves its first flight, an event that marks the time since birth at fledging as approximately 76 days [tx = approximately 76 days] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This extended nestling period is among the longest recorded for cockatoos of comparable body mass, reflecting the slow pace of feather development and the gradual strengthening of flight muscles required for a large-bodied bird. During this time, the parents deliver a diet consisting primarily of seeds from native eucalypts and she-oaks, which provides the necessary nutrients for skeletal growth and the development of the distinctive yellow tail feathers. The fledgling, upon leaving the hollow, remains in close association with its parents for several additional weeks, during which it continues to be provisioned while refining its foraging skills and flight capabilities in the surrounding forest canopy.

Sexual maturation in the Yellow-tailed black cockatoo is a relatively slow process, with puberty estimated to occur at 228 days since birth [tp = 228 days since birth] under thermoneutral conditions of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This figure, however, marks only the onset of gonadal development and the production of viable gametes, rather than the immediate commencement of breeding activity. Young birds typically delay their first reproductive attempt for several years after reaching physiological puberty, as they must first acquire the social status, foraging proficiency, and a suitable nest hollow within their complex, long-term pair bonds. The protracted delay between sexual maturation and actual reproduction is a common life-history strategy among large, long-lived parrots, allowing individuals to invest in somatic growth and behavioral experience before committing to the substantial energetic demands of incubation and chick-rearing. Observational data from banded populations suggest that many immature individuals do not begin actively prospecting for nest sites until well after their second or third year of life, highlighting a clear distinction between physiological readiness and ecological opportunity.

At a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the age at first reproduction for this species, representing the time since birth at first brood, has been documented as 4 years since birth [tR = 4 years since birth]. This delayed onset of breeding is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival and iteroparity over early, potentially costly, reproductive effort. Females typically produce a single clutch per breeding season, laying 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch], and the species generally raises only one clutch each year [F_R_i = one clutch each year]. The maximum reproductive rate is thus constrained by both the small clutch size and the infrequent breeding events, a pattern that reflects the unpredictable availability of the large tree hollows required for nesting and the extended period of parental dependency. In years of poor food abundance, breeding may be entirely foregone, further emphasizing the conservative reproductive strategy that buffers the population against environmental stochasticity. This low annual fecundity is offset by high adult survival and a remarkable maximum lifespan, which together ensure population stability over the long term.

The maximum recorded lifespan for the Yellow-tailed black cockatoo is approximately 41 years [am = approximately 41 years] based on data from wild individuals studied at a body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This exceptional longevity is among the greatest documented for any member of the Cacatuidae and is coupled with a correspondingly slow growth and developmental trajectory. Adults attain an ultimate wet weight of 800 grams [Wwi = 800 grams] for females, while males are slightly smaller, reaching a maximum recorded adult body mass of 731 grams [Wwi = 731 grams]. The initial wet weight recorded for newly hatched chicks is 33.8 grams [Ww0 = 33.8 grams], a value that represents the mass of the embryo immediately upon emergence from the egg, distinct from the slightly lower wet weight at birth recorded after the first few hours of drying. This combination of a high adult mass, a slow developmental rate, and a very long lifespan positions the species firmly within the slow end of the life-history continuum for parrots, a strategy that has proven successful across its range in southeastern Australia despite ongoing pressures from habitat loss and competition for nesting hollows.
